fixes.explanation: That's a fair guess after all those lines about sons and daughters. But the text says, “But Sarai was barren; she had no children.” No children means no daughter either. The writer has been giving fathers and their sons and daughters, then stops on her with one short sentence, and it stands out.

I see why that sounds believable, since Lot's father Haran has died. But the text says Terah took “his grandson Lot son of Haran” along with Abram and Sarai. Lot is part of the group that sets out from Ur of the Chaldeans. He gets a spot in the lineup.

That's right! The text says that when they arrived in Haran, they settled there. It's the same name as Terah's son Haran, who died in Ur, so keep them straight: one is a man and one is a place. They set out for Canaan, and this is where they stop instead.

Babel is where the LORD confused the language of the whole world (Genesis 11:9). It comes up just before this passage, but it isn't where this family settles. The text says they settle in Haran. Same book, different stop on the map, friend.

Nineveh is the great city God sends Jonah to (Jonah 1:2). It never comes up in this passage. The text says that when Terah's family arrives in Haran, they settle there. Nineveh belongs to a different story.

Nope, no trip back. The text says Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran. Ur is where the family set out from, and the text never has him return there. I think this one is a heavy line, and the writer states it plainly.

That's right, baker! God says, “…go to the land I will show you.” No map and no address, just a promise to show him. That takes real trust, friend. I'd have asked for directions twice and then packed extra cookie boxes.

That's it, friend! God says, “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you…” And remember, Sarai has no children yet. That's like holding one lonely cookie and being told it will feed a stadium. Only God can make a promise that size.

Yes, baker. God says, “I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.” Notice the “so that.” The name is tied to being a blessing. That's how God puts it, and the very next thing He says is that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram.

I see why you'd pick it, since Abram is the one the blessing comes through. But God says, “…all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” That's a much bigger circle than one household. It reaches every family on earth.

That's right, baker. Abram travels through the land as far as the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. The text then adds that the Canaanites were in the land at that time. So the land isn't empty, and Abram arrives where other people already are.

A city is a big project, but the text doesn't say Abram builds one. It says, “So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.” What goes up is an altar, built to the LORD. That's the only thing the text says he builds there.

That's right, friend! The text says Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent. Then, “There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.” That makes a second altar in the land, after the one where the LORD appeared to him.
